title: Python Start: Interpreter, Environments & PyCharm
sub: Install, run, isolate and debug your first Python programs in Terminal and PyCharm
goals: Identify which Python your Mac runs and why, and avoid touching Apple's copy
Use the REPL and run code with python3 file.py, -c and -m
Create, activate and rebuild a virtual environment with venv and pip
Create a PyCharm project, pick its interpreter and use Run, the Terminal and the Python Console
Read input with input(), print results and build a small stdin-driven units tool

blocks.text: You already know how a shell turns text into processes. Python is the next layer up: a program that reads text (your source code), turns it into instructions and executes them, all inside one process you can start with `python3`. By the end of this chapter you will run Python five different ways, keep each project's packages in its own sandbox, and have PyCharm set up so that pressing one button runs the same interpreter you would run in Terminal.

blocks.title: Two places to run Python in this book

blocks.text: Code in a **run** block (it has a Run button) executes in your browser using CPython compiled to WebAssembly. It is real Python 3.13, but it has no network, no sockets and no access to your files. Code in a **file** or **python** block is meant for your Mac: save it, then run it with Terminal or PyCharm. When a block can run in the page, edit it and press Run. Break it on purpose. Nothing here can hurt anything.

blocks.code:
import sys
print("Hello from", sys.implementation.name)
print(2 ** 100)

blocks.text: The second line is worth a pause: Python computed 2 to the 100th power exactly. Python integers have no fixed size, they grow as needed, which is why it is a good language for experiments with addresses, masks and hashes.
Which Python is this?

Your Mac can have several Pythons at once. Programs on your `PATH` named `python3` are found in order, exactly as you learned in [zsh basics](#zsh-basics), so the first question in any Python problem is always: *which one am I running?*

blocks.code:
which -a python3
python3 -V
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.prefix)'

blocks.text: `which -a` lists every match on `PATH`, not just the first. `-V` prints the version. The `-c` form runs a string of code and exits; `sys.executable` is the real path of the running interpreter and `sys.prefix` is the folder it treats as its home.

head: Source
Typical path of `python3`
Use it for
rows: Apple's own scripts. Leave it alone. It is a small launcher that may prompt to install the developer tools, and it is an older version (3.9 at the time of writing).
Official builds, bundled Tcl/Tk for `tkinter`, includes `Install Certificates.command`
The easiest to update with `brew upgrade`. Marked "externally managed" (see below)
Per-project interpreters you never put on `PATH` yourself

blocks.text: Pick one system Python for your Terminal (Homebrew is the least effort if you already installed Homebrew in [Setup](#setup)), and let every project create its own virtual environment on top of it. Do not edit, upgrade or delete anything under `/usr/bin` or `/System`: macOS itself depends on it, and System Integrity Protection blocks most changes anyway.

On a fresh Mac, `python` (without the 3) is not found. Scripts and tutorials that say `python` assume Linux or a virtual environment, where `python` is a link to the interpreter that built the environment. In this book you type `python3` in Terminal and plain `python` only after activating a venv.

This book is written for Python 3.12 or newer, and the in-page runner is 3.13. Everything except a few clearly marked features works on 3.10 and later. `match` needs 3.10, `ExceptionGroup` and `tomllib` need 3.11, and the newer REPL described below arrives in 3.13. As of October 2026 the newest stable series is 3.15, and Homebrew's `python` formula installs it. Check python.org for the current release when you install.

blocks.text: The REPL: Python as a calculator and a microscope
Run `python3` with no arguments and you get the **REPL** (read, evaluate, print, loop). Python reads one statement, runs it, prints the value, and waits for the next.

blocks.code:
$ python3
Python 3.13.2 (main, Feb  4 2025, 14:51:09) [Clang 16.0.0] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> 6 * 7
42
>>> _ + 1
43
>>> name = "router"
>>> name.upper()
'ROUTER'
>>> for i in range(2):
...     print(i)
...
0
1
>>> dir(name)[-3:]
['translate', 'upper', 'zfill']
>>> exit()

items.text: The first line names the version, when it was built and the compiler used. This sample came from a 3.13 install; with Homebrew's current Python it starts `Python 3.15`.
`>>>` is the primary prompt, `...` the continuation prompt for an indented block. Finish a block with an empty line.
The REPL echoes the **repr** of any expression whose value is not `None`. `print()` is only needed in scripts.
`_` holds the last printed value. Use it to chain quick calculations.
`help(x)` shows documentation for an object, `dir(x)` lists its attributes, `type(x)` names its type. These three answer most "what can I do with this?" questions.
Leave with `exit()` or [[Ctrl+D]] (end of input, the same signal that ends `cat` or `sort`).
`python3 -i script.py` runs a script and then drops into the REPL with all its variables still defined. It is the quickest debugger there is.

blocks.text: From 3.13 the REPL supports multi-line editing, coloured prompts, `F2` for browsable history and `F3` for paste mode, and `exit` or `quit` work without parentheses. Earlier versions need `exit()`. If your REPL looks plainer than the one above, you are on an older version.
The REPL is also where you test one idea at a time before putting it in a file. The playground below behaves like a REPL for whole scripts: edit, press Run, read the output.

blocks.text: Create your first script. Use PyCharm if it is open, or `nano` in Terminal.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print a greeting and the arguments the program received."""
import sys

print("hello,", "world")
print("arguments:", sys.argv[1:])
python3 hello.py one two three

blocks.text: You should see `hello, world` and `arguments: ['one', 'two', 'three']`. `sys.argv` is the list of command-line words: element 0 is the script name, the rest are your arguments, exactly like `$0` and `$1...` in a shell script.
Making a script directly executable

The first line `#!/usr/bin/env python3` is a **shebang**. When the kernel is asked to execute a file that starts with `#!`, it launches the named program and passes the file to it. `/usr/bin/env python3` means "find `python3` on `PATH`", which respects an activated venv, instead of hard-coding one interpreter path.

blocks.code:
chmod +x hello.py
./hello.py a b

blocks.text: Without `chmod +x` you get `zsh: permission denied: ./hello.py`, the execute bit lesson from [Files](#files). Put executable scripts in `~/bin` (on your `PATH` from the [Scripting](#scripting) chapter) and they behave like any other command.
Python inside pipelines

Python reads stdin and writes stdout like every other tool, so it slots into the pipelines from [Streams and pipes](#pipes). When `awk` or `cut` would get awkward, a few lines of Python finish the job.

blocks.code:
echo "10.0.0.5" | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.stdin.read().strip().split(".")[-1])'
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sum(1 for _ in sys.stdin))' < access.log
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort -u | python3 -c 'import sys; print(len(sys.stdin.read().split()))'

blocks.text: The first prints the last octet (`5`), the second counts lines (120 for the lab log, the same as `wc -l`), the third counts unique IPs. Python exits with status 0 when the program finishes normally and 1 when it ends with an uncaught exception, so `&&` and `||` work with it too.

blocks.text: Packages and virtual environments

Python ships with a large standard library (`json`, `socket`, `re`, `ipaddress` and more), and the rest of the world lives on **PyPI**, the Python Package Index. `pip` downloads packages from PyPI. The problem: if every project installs into one shared place, `project A` wants `requests 2.28`, `project B` wants `2.32`, and one of them breaks. A **virtual environment** (venv) fixes that by giving each project its own private `site-packages` folder and its own copy of the interpreter link.

blocks.code:
my-project/
  ├── main.py
  ├── requirements.txt          <- the list of packages the project needs
  └── .venv/                    <- the sandbox (never commit this folder)
      ├── pyvenv.cfg            <- records which base Python made it
      ├── bin/
      │   ├── python  ──────────▶ link to the base interpreter
      │   ├── python3
      │   ├── pip
      │   └── activate          <- script you `source` to enter the sandbox
      └── lib/python3.13/site-packages/
          ├── requests/         <- packages installed by `pip` land here
          └── ...

blocks.text: What activation does

`source .venv/bin/activate` does very little: it puts `.venv/bin` at the **front** of `PATH`, sets `VIRTUAL_ENV`, and prefixes your prompt with `(.venv)`. After that, `python`, `python3` and `pip` resolve to the sandbox copies because the shell finds them first. `deactivate` undoes it. You can skip activation completely by calling `.venv/bin/python` directly, which is what PyCharm and cron jobs do.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab && mkdir py-demo && cd py-demo
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ which python3
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python3
/Users/me/lab/py-demo/.venv/bin/python3
(.venv) $ python3 -m pip install --quiet rich
(.venv) $ pip list
Package         Version
--------------- -------
markdown-it-py  4.0.0
mdurl           0.1.2
pip             25.3
Pygments        2.19.2
rich            14.2.0
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python3
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3

blocks.text: Homebrew's Python (and most Linux distributions' Python) is marked as owned by its package manager. A global `pip install` fails on purpose:

blocks.code:
error: externally-managed-environment

× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try brew install xyz ...
    If you wish to install a Python library that isn't in Homebrew,
    use a virtual environment ...

blocks.text: The fix is the venv above, not `--break-system-packages`. That flag works, and it also lets you wreck the interpreter Homebrew's own tools use. For command-line applications written in Python, `pipx install <app>` (via `brew install pipx`) gives each app its own venv. `uv` (via `brew install uv`) is a much faster all-in-one replacement for `venv` plus `pip`; the commands in this book work with either.
Recording what a project needs

blocks.code:
python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt     # exact versions of everything installed
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt   # rebuild the same environment elsewhere

blocks.text: A good habit: because `.venv` can be rebuilt in seconds from `requirements.txt`, you can delete it any time something feels broken (`rm -rf .venv`, create it again, reinstall). Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore` so it never enters version control, and commit `requirements.txt` instead (the git workflow is in [Thinking like a programmer](#thinking)).

`python3 -m pip install x` runs the pip that belongs to *that* interpreter, so the package lands where you expect. A bare `pip` is whichever one is first on `PATH`, which on a Mac is sometimes attached to a different Python. Inside an activated venv they agree, outside it only `python3 -m pip` is safe to trust.

blocks.name: python3
blocks.sum: Start the Python interpreter: the REPL with no arguments, or run a file, a string of code or a module.

how.text: `python3` loads your source, compiles it to bytecode in memory, and runs that bytecode in a virtual machine, all in one process. Everything after the program name is passed in `sys.argv`, so `python3 hello.py a b` gives the script `['hello.py', 'a', 'b']`. The exit status is 0 on normal completion, 1 after an uncaught exception, or whatever you pass to `sys.exit(n)`.

With `-m`, Python searches `sys.path` for a module and runs it as `__main__`. That is how you launch tools that live inside a package without knowing where the package is installed: `python3 -m venv`, `python3 -m http.server`, `python3 -m pytest`.

flags.d: Run CODE (a string) and exit. Quote it for zsh.
Run library module MOD as a script (`-m http.server`).
Print the version and exit (`-VV` adds build details).
After running a script or `-c`, open the REPL with its variables still alive.
Do not buffer stdout and stderr. Useful when piping a long-running script to `tee` or `grep`.
Isolated mode: ignore `PYTHON*` environment variables and the current directory. Safer for untrusted folders.

gotchas: Output is block-buffered when stdout is a pipe or file, so a slow script piped into `grep` seems silent. Use `python3 -u` or `print(..., flush=True)`.
A file named like a standard module (`random.py`, `socket.py`, `json.py`) in your folder shadows the real module and causes baffling errors. Never name your scripts after library modules.

blocks.name: venv
blocks.sum: Create an isolated Python environment with its own site-packages in a folder.

how.text: The `venv` module creates `DIR`, copies or links the interpreter into `DIR/bin`, writes `pyvenv.cfg` and creates an empty `site-packages`. It does not copy the standard library. Activation is optional convenience: it prepends `DIR/bin` to `PATH` so `python` and `pip` resolve there. Delete the folder to delete the environment.

flags.d: Empty the folder first if it exists.
Upgrade pip inside the new environment to the latest version.
Let the environment also see packages from the base Python. Rarely needed.

Leave it

gotchas: `source .venv/bin/activate` only affects the current Terminal tab. A new tab starts without it, so check the `(.venv)` prefix in the prompt.
Moving or renaming a project folder breaks the venv, because scripts inside contain absolute paths. Recreate it instead.

blocks.name: pip
blocks.sum: Install, list and remove Python packages from PyPI into the current environment.

how.text: `pip` resolves a package name to the newest compatible version on PyPI, downloads it with its dependencies and unpacks it into the active environment's `site-packages`. Version specifiers use `==` (exact), `>=` (at least) and `~=` (compatible): `pip install 'requests>=2.31,<3'`. Quote them so zsh does not read `>` as a redirect.

Show installed packages. `--outdated` shows those with newer versions.
Version, dependencies and install location of one package.

`pip install` runs code from the package author. Install only packages you recognize, and check the exact spelling: look-alike names are a real attack.

blocks.text: PyCharm in practice

PyCharm is an IDE (integrated development environment): an editor that understands Python, plus a runner, debugger, terminal, package manager and version control in one window. Install it as described in [Setup](#setup). The free tier is enough for everything in this book. Menu names change slightly between releases, but the ideas below do not.
Create a project

items.text: Choose **File | New Project** (or **New Project** on the welcome screen).
Set **Location** to a folder, for example `~/lab/hello-py`. The project is named after the folder.

Under the interpreter options choose **Project venv**. PyCharm runs `python -m venv .venv` inside the project for you and selects it. (Other options are **uv**, **Conda** and **Custom environment** for an interpreter you already have.) On macOS the dialog can also download a Python build for you.
Tick **Create a main.py welcome script** if you want a starter file, then **Create**.

blocks.text: Look at the bottom-right corner of the window: it shows the active interpreter (for example `Python 3.13 (hello-py)`). Click it to switch interpreters or **Add New Interpreter**. The same settings live in **Settings | Project | Python Interpreter** (`⌘,`), where the list of installed packages is also shown and edited.
Run and debug

macOS shortcut
Notes
rows: Or click the green triangle in the gutter next to `if __name__ == "__main__":`
Stops at breakpoints (click the gutter to set one, covered in [Errors](#py-errors))

blocks.text: The first run creates a **run configuration** (the drop-down at the top right). Open **Edit Configurations** to see what it stores: the script path, **Parameters** (the words that become `sys.argv`), **Working directory**, **Environment variables** and which interpreter to use. When a program behaves differently in PyCharm and in Terminal, the cause is almost always a different interpreter or working directory in this dialog.
The tool windows you will use daily

items.text: **Terminal**: a real zsh session opened in the project folder. When the project has a venv, PyCharm activates it for you, so `python3 -m pip install` and `python3 file.py` use the project's environment. Use this for everything shell-shaped in this book.

**Python Console**: a REPL attached to the project interpreter. Select code in the editor, right-click, **Execute Selection in Python Console**, then keep exploring the variables in the console and the variable viewer next to it. If you cannot see it, use **View | Tool Windows | Python Console**.
**Python Packages**: search PyPI, install and uninstall into the active interpreter without typing `pip`. It does the same thing as the Terminal commands; knowing both helps when one fails.
**Run**: the output of the last run, with clickable file and line numbers in tracebacks.

blocks.text: If `python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'` printed in PyCharm's Terminal ends with `.venv/bin/python3`, the Terminal, the Run button and the Python Console are all using one sandbox. Check this first whenever "it works in one place but not the other".
First programs: output, input and arithmetic
A program is a list of statements run from top to bottom. The three you need immediately are `print`, `input` and assignment.

blocks.code:
name = "gateway"
octets = 4
print("host:", name)
print("octets:", octets, "bits:", octets * 8)
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
print("no newline", end=" | ")
print("same line")
blocks.out:
host: gateway
octets: 4 bits: 32
a-b-c
no newline | same line

blocks.text: `name = "gateway"` binds a **name** to a value. There is no declaration and no type annotation required: the value has a type, the name does not. `print` converts each argument with `str()`, joins them with `sep` (a space by default) and ends with `end` (a newline by default).
Python's arithmetic operators behave like a calculator with two extras, floor division `//` and remainder `%`, which networking code uses constantly:

blocks.code:
print(17 / 5)      # true division always gives a float
print(17 // 5)     # floor division
print(17 % 5)      # remainder
print(2 ** 10)     # power
print(divmod(17, 5))
print(round(3.14159, 2))

blocks.text: `input()` pauses and reads one line from stdin, returning it as a **string**, even if the user types digits. Converting is your job. This is the single most common beginner error, so make it break once on purpose:

blocks.code:
seconds = input("seconds? ")
print("minutes:", seconds / 60)

blocks.text: The page shows a `TypeError`: you cannot divide a string by an integer. Fix it by converting first, with `int()` for whole numbers or `float()` for decimals:

blocks.code:
seconds = int(input("seconds? "))
print("minutes:", seconds / 60)
print("whole minutes and leftover seconds:", divmod(seconds, 60))
blocks.out:
seconds? minutes: 1.5
whole minutes and leftover seconds: (1, 30)

blocks.text: The prompt text appears without a newline, so in a terminal the answer is typed right after it; here the output shows both lines run together because the "typed" text comes from the stdin box.

Everything after `#` on a line is ignored by Python. Use comments to explain *why*, not to repeat *what*. A triple-quoted string as the first statement of a file or function is a **docstring**, which `help()` displays.

blocks.name: print()
blocks.sum: Write values to stdout (or another file), separated by `sep` and ended with `end`.

how.text: `print` calls `str()` on every argument, writes them with `sep` between and `end` after, and returns `None`. It writes to `sys.stdout` unless you pass `file=`, so `print("oops", file=sys.stderr)` sends a message to the error stream instead, the stderr channel from [Streams and pipes](#pipes). In a pipe the output is block-buffered; `flush=True` forces it out immediately.

examples.desc: Separators, line endings and the error stream
Emit a CSV line from a script and sort it in the shell
examples.code: python3 -c 'for h, p in [("pi", 22), ("nas", 445)]: print(h, p, sep=",")' | sort

gotchas: `print` is a function in Python 3. The Python 2 form `print "x"` is a SyntaxError.

blocks.name: input()
blocks.sum: Read one line from stdin and return it as a string without the trailing newline.

how.text: `input` writes `prompt` (without a newline) to stdout, reads a line from stdin and strips the newline. At end of input it raises `EOFError`. The result is always `str`, so wrap it in `int()` or `float()` when you need a number. For many lines or piped data, read `sys.stdin` directly instead (shown in the project below).

examples.desc: Ask for a number and double it
Feed the answer from another command

gotchas: The answer is text: `input() + 1` is a TypeError, and `input() * 3` repeats the text three times.

blocks.name: help()
blocks.sum: Show the documentation of an object, a module or a keyword.

how.text: `help` is the interactive front end to the `pydoc` module. It reads docstrings and signatures from live objects, so it always matches the version you run. On a terminal long output opens in a pager (`q` to leave, `/` to search). The same text is available from the shell with `python3 -m pydoc NAME`.

Help on built-in function len in module builtins:

len(obj, /)
    Return the number of items in a container.

examples.desc: Read docs from the shell without entering Python

blocks.name: dir()
blocks.sum: List the names an object offers, or the names in the current scope when called with no argument.

how.text: `dir` returns a sorted list of attribute names: the methods and fields you can use on the object. Names with double underscores are the protocol hooks Python itself calls (`__len__`, `__add__`); filter them out to see the useful ones.

examples.desc: Which str methods start with "is"?
examples.code: print([n for n in dir("") if n.startswith("is")])

examples.desc: Print one method name per line and search it

blocks.name: type()
blocks.sum: Return the type (class) of an object.

how.text: Every value is an object with exactly one type, and the type decides which operations work. `type` is how you check what you actually have: after `input()` it is `str`, after division it is `float`. For tests inside programs prefer `isinstance`, which also accepts subclasses.

examples.desc: Types of common values
examples.code:
print(type(42), type(4.2), type("42"), type(True), type(None))
print(type([1]), type((1,)), type({1: 2}), type({1}))

examples.desc: Show the type of whatever a shell variable parses as

blocks.name: id()
blocks.sum: Return an integer that uniquely identifies an object for as long as it exists.

how.text: In CPython `id` is the object's memory address. Two names with the same `id` are two labels on one object, which matters for mutable values such as lists. Use it to learn how assignment works, not to build program logic.

examples.desc: Two names, one list

gotchas: Never compare ids to test equality. `==` asks "same value?" and `is` asks "same object?".

blocks.text: Useful modules you can run with -m
`python3 -m name` turns the standard library into a toolbox. Each of these works in a plain Terminal with no installs.

head: Command
What it gives you
rows: A static web server for the current folder on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Perfect for practising `curl`
Validates and pretty-prints JSON from a file or stdin (`--sort-keys`, `--compact`)
The package installer for that interpreter
Searches all documentation for a keyword. `-b` opens a browser documentation server
Times a statement by running it many times and reporting the best average
Prints "The Zen of Python", the language's design principles

blocks.code: python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

blocks.text: Leave that running in one Terminal tab and, in another, run `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. You have just built your first server and watched a real HTTP exchange against it.

Without `--bind 127.0.0.1` the server listens on every interface, so anyone on your Wi-Fi can read the folder you started it in. Start it only in a folder whose contents you are happy to share, and stop it with [[Ctrl+C]]. It has no authentication and no hardening, so it is never a production server.

blocks.code:
$ python3 -m timeit 'sum(range(1000))'
20000 loops, best of 5: 10.4 usec per loop
$ python3 -m timeit -s 'data = list(range(1000))' '999 in data'
50000 loops, best of 5: 6.4 usec per loop
$ echo '{"b": 2, "a": [1, 2]}' | python3 -m json.tool --sort-keys
{
    "a": [
        1,
        2
    ],
    "b": 2
}

blocks.text: `timeit` picks a loop count that takes at least 0.2 seconds, repeats five times and reports the best, which filters out noise from other processes. `-s` runs setup code once, outside the timing.
Writing code other people can read

Python's layout rules are part of the language: a block is whatever is indented the same amount after a colon. Mix tabs and spaces or indent inconsistently and you get an `IndentationError`. Beyond that, the community follows **PEP 8**, the official style guide. PyCharm flags violations with a wavy underline and `⌥⌘L` fixes most of them.

head: Rule
Example
rows: Lines up to about 79 to 100 characters
Two blank lines around top-level functions, one between methods
Imports at the top, one per line, grouped: standard library, third party, yours
Spaces around operators and after commas, none inside brackets
Names say what the value is

blocks.text: Formatters settle style arguments automatically: **ruff** (`ruff format`, `ruff check`, installable with `python3 -m pip install ruff` inside a venv) and **black** apply one consistent layout. You do not need either today. When you do, run them from the PyCharm Terminal.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Running the file from the wrong folder.** `python3: can't open file '/Users/me/hello.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory` means the path is wrong, not Python. `pwd`, `ls`, then retry.
**Installing with the wrong pip.** The package installs somewhere, then `ModuleNotFoundError` appears. Use `python3 -m pip` and check `which python3`.
**Forgetting to activate (or deactivate) the venv.** Look for `(.venv)` in your prompt.
**Naming a script `random.py`, `json.py` or `socket.py`.** It shadows the library module of the same name.
**Copying code with curly quotes.** `SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)` means a word processor or web page replaced straight quotes. Retype them.
**Mixing tabs and spaces.** PyCharm converts for you; configure your editor to insert spaces.
**Assuming `input()` returns a number.** It returns text. Convert it.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Find out which Python you are running

task.text: In Terminal, run one command that lists **every** `python3` on your `PATH`, then print the version of the first one, and finally print where that interpreter says its home folder is (`sys.prefix`). Decide, from the paths, which of the sources in the table above each one is.

hints: `which` has a flag that does not stop at the first match.
`python3 -V` prints the version, `python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.prefix)'` prints the prefix.
blocks.solution:
which -a python3
python3 -V
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.prefix)'

why.text: `which -a` shows the search order that `PATH` imposes, so the first line is the one that runs. If the first one is `/usr/bin/python3`, install Homebrew's Python or the python.org build and make sure its folder comes earlier on `PATH`.

blocks.verify: python3 -c 'import sys; print("OK" if sys.version_info >= (3, 9) else "old")'

blocks.title: Venv round trip

task.text: In `~/lab`, create a folder `py-demo`, make a virtual environment `.venv` inside it, activate it, install `rich`, write the installed packages to `requirements.txt`, deactivate, delete the venv with `rm -rf .venv` (look at what you are deleting first with `ls`), then rebuild it from `requirements.txt` and confirm `rich` is available.

hints: `python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt` records it. After recreating the venv, `python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt` restores it.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab && mkdir -p py-demo && cd py-demo
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install rich
python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
deactivate
ls .venv
rm -rf .venv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 -c 'import rich; print("rich ok")'

why.text: The venv is disposable because `requirements.txt` fully describes it. This is the reproducibility habit: another Mac, a fresh clone or next year's you can rebuild the same environment with two commands.

blocks.verify: grep -qi '^rich==' requirements.txt && echo "OK: rich is pinned"

blocks.title: Break it, read it, fix it

task.text: Save this as `broken.py` and run it with `python3 broken.py`. It has two different bugs. Fix the first error Python reports, run again, then fix the second. The program must finally print `total: 6`.

hints: Read the last line of the error first: it names the kind of error. The line above it says where.
The first is an `IndentationError` (the body of `for` must be indented one level deeper). The second is a `NameError` caused by a typo.

why.text: Python checks syntax and indentation for the whole file before running anything, so the `IndentationError` appears first. The `NameError` only appears when execution reaches the misspelled name. Both messages tell you the line and the exact problem: that habit of reading the last line first will serve you for the rest of the book.

blocks.title: Temperature function

task.text: Write `c_to_f(c)` that converts degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit (`F = C * 9 / 5 + 32`) and returns the number.

why.text: `c * 9 / 5 + 32` follows ordinary precedence: multiplication and division first, left to right, then addition. The function returns the value instead of printing it, so other code can reuse it.

blocks.check:
assert c_to_f(0) == 32, "0 C should be 32 F"
assert c_to_f(100) == 212, "100 C should be 212 F"
assert abs(c_to_f(-40) - (-40)) < 1e-9, "-40 is the same in both scales"
assert abs(c_to_f(36.6) - 97.88) < 1e-9, "36.6 C should be 97.88 F"

blocks.title: Sum and product from stdin

task.text: Read two whole numbers, each on its own line, using `input()`. Print exactly one line in the form `sum=13 product=42` (for 6 and 7).

blocks.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print("sum=" + str(a + b), "product=" + str(a * b))

why.text: `input()` returns strings, so both values need `int()` before arithmetic. `print` with two arguments puts a space between them, which gives the required format.

blocks.check: assert out.strip() == "sum=13 product=42", "expected 'sum=13 product=42' but got " + repr(out.strip())

blocks.title: Python as a pipeline stage

task.text: Without using `wc`, count the lines of `access.log` with a `python3 -c` one-liner that reads `sys.stdin`, feeding the file in with `<`. Then check your answer against `wc -l < access.log`.

hints: `sys.stdin` can be iterated line by line, or read at once with `.readlines()`.
blocks.solution:
python3 -c 'import sys; print(len(sys.stdin.readlines()))' < access.log
wc -l < access.log

why.text: Python treats stdin as a file object. `.readlines()` returns a list of lines, and `len` counts them. Anything the shell can pipe into `wc` it can pipe into Python, which makes Python the escape hatch whenever a one-liner outgrows `awk`.

questions.q: Why create a virtual environment for each project?

options.text: Each project gets its own packages, so versions cannot clash and the folder can be deleted and rebuilt
It is required before you can run any script

questions.why: A venv is isolation and reproducibility. It does not speed anything up, and scripts run fine without one until a package conflict or an externally-managed error appears.

options.text: It puts `.venv/bin` at the front of `PATH` and sets `VIRTUAL_ENV`, so `python` and `pip` resolve inside the venv
It starts a second Terminal app

questions.why: Activation is a small shell trick on `PATH`. Calling `.venv/bin/python` directly gets the same result without it.

questions.q: What type does `input()` return when the user types 42?
questions.why: `input()` always returns text. Use `int("42")` or `float("42")` to get a number.

questions.q: Which command runs the standard-library JSON pretty-printer on stdin?
questions.why: `-m` runs a module found on `sys.path` as a script. Without it Python would look for a file called `json.tool`.

questions.q: Your script works in PyCharm's Run button but fails with ModuleNotFoundError in a fresh Terminal tab. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The script has a syntax error
The Terminal tab is using a different Python than the project's venv

questions.why: Different interpreter, different `site-packages`. Activate the venv or run `.venv/bin/python script.py`, and compare `which python3` in both places.

questions.q: What does the first line `#!/usr/bin/env python3` do?

options.text: It is a comment Python reads for the version
It tells the kernel which interpreter to launch when the file is executed directly, found through PATH

questions.why: The kernel reads the `#!` line when you run `./script.py` (after `chmod +x`) and starts the named program with the file as its argument.

blocks.text: Build `units.py`, a small command that reads lines such as `72 F` or `5 km` from standard input and prints the converted value. It starts as a tested function in the page and ends as an executable filter that works in a pipeline.
Step 1: One conversion in the page
Edit and run this. The function takes the text of one line and returns the answer as a string. Add conversions of your own: miles to kilometres is `1.609344`, pounds to kilograms is `0.45359237`.

blocks.out:
100 C -> 212.0 F
72 F -> 22.2 C
5 km -> 3.11 mi
26.2 mi -> 42.16 km
3 parsec -> unknown unit parsec

blocks.text: `line.split()` breaks a string on whitespace into a list, and the two names on the left unpack that two-item list. The f-string `f"{x:.1f}"` formats a float to one decimal place. Both are covered fully in [Basics](#py-basics).
Step 2: Turn it into a filter
A filter reads lines from stdin and writes results to stdout. Save this as `units.py`:

blocks.code:
chmod +x units.py
printf '100 C
72 F
5 km
' | ./units.py

blocks.text: `for line in sys.stdin` hands you one line at a time, including its trailing newline, so `strip()` removes it. The `if line:` skips blank lines. Because it reads stdin and writes stdout it composes with everything from the shell chapters: `./units.py < temps.txt | sort -k4 -n`.
Step 3: Make it robust

Run `echo "banana" | ./units.py` and read the traceback: `split()` returned one word, so the unpacking failed with `ValueError`. Handling that cleanly needs `try/except`, which [Errors](#py-errors) teaches. For now, add a guard before the call: skip any line that does not contain exactly two words, and print a message to `sys.stderr` with `print(..., file=sys.stderr)` so bad input does not pollute the results in a pipeline.

Add `kg` and `lb`, then `m` and `ft`. Allow `--to` style flags later with `argparse` ([Modules](#py-modules)). Put the conversion table in a dictionary instead of an `if` chain once you have read [Data structures](#py-data).
Next: [Python basics](#py-basics) takes numbers, text and operators apart in depth, with a reference card for every built-in function and string method.

terms.def: Read-evaluate-print loop: the interactive Python prompt where each statement runs as soon as you press Enter
The program (`python3`) that reads your source code and executes it
A virtual environment: a folder holding a private set of installed packages and a link to a base interpreter
The Python Package Index, the public repository that `pip` installs from
Python's package installer; run it as `python3 -m pip`
The `#!` first line of a script that names the interpreter the kernel should launch
Python Enhancement Proposal: a numbered design document, such as PEP 8 (style) and PEP 668 (externally managed environments)
A string literal as the first statement of a module or function, shown by `help()`
The report Python prints for an uncaught exception, listing the calls that led to it, with the error on the last line
Environment variable listing extra folders Python searches for modules, after the script's own folder
PyCharm's saved settings for one launch: script, parameters, working directory, environment and interpreter
